title: Quadriceps femoris
source: OpenStax A&P 2e: 11.6 Appendicular Muscles of the Pelvic Girdle and Lower Limbs; 11.1; 13.4; 14.3; 16.4

main.t: The group of four muscles at the front of the thigh that extend and stabilise the knee.

simpler.t: The quadriceps are the big muscles on the front of your thigh. They straighten your knee.

deeper.t: All four join one tendon to the patella, which continues as the patellar ligament to the tibial tuberosity.

facts.t: They fill the anterior compartment of the thigh.
Rectus femoris lies in front, vastus lateralis on the outer side and vastus medialis on the inner side. Vastus intermedius lies between them, deep.

simpler.t: They cover the front and sides of your thigh, above the kneecap.

deeper.t: Only the rectus femoris arises from the hip bone; the three vasti arise from the femur.

items.name: Rectus femoris
items.t: Arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine and above the acetabulum. It also helps raise the knee.

items.name: Vastus lateralis
items.t: Arises from the greater trochanter, the intertrochanteric line and the linea aspera.

items.name: Vastus medialis
items.t: Arises from the linea aspera and the intertrochanteric line.

items.name: Vastus intermedius
items.t: Arises from the upper shaft of the femur, deep to the rectus femoris.

items.name: Quadriceps tendon
items.t: The tendon common to all four. It inserts into the patella.

simpler.t: Four muscles, one shared tendon, one kneecap.

deeper.t: Their motor units are large, up to about 1,000 fibres each, suited to force rather than fine control.

facts.t: Pulling through the patella and patellar ligament, they extend the leg at the knee, as in kicking.
The rectus femoris crosses the hip too, so it also flexes the thigh.
The hamstrings, behind, are their antagonists.

simpler.t: They straighten the knee; the front one also lifts the thigh.

items.name: Patella
items.t: Lies in the quadriceps tendon. The tendon continues below it as the patellar ligament.

items.name: Hamstrings
items.t: In the posterior compartment. They flex the knee, opposing the quadriceps.

items.name: Sartorius
items.t: A band-like muscle crossing the front of the thigh, also in the anterior compartment.

items.name: Femoral nerve
items.t: A major nerve of the lumbar plexus, to the front of the thigh.
items.check: Not in OpenStax A&P 2e (chapters 6–17, 19–23 and 25). That the femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps.

simpler.t: They pull on the kneecap and are opposed by the hamstrings.

facts.t: Limb muscles develop from general mesoderm. Satellite cells later repair the fibres.
Without use, they waste quickly (disuse atrophy), for example after a leg fracture.
Age-related loss (sarcopenia) is slowed, though not stopped, by exercise.

items.injury: Damage to the quadriceps’ reflex arc: its sensory fibres, the spinal cord or its lower motor neurons.
items.damaged: The knee-jerk (stretch) reflex of the quadriceps.
items.cannotDo: Kick the leg forwards when the patellar ligament is tapped.
items.why: The tap normally stretches the muscle, and its spindles excite its motor neurons directly.

items.injury: A leg kept in plaster for weeks.
items.cannotDo: Straighten the knee strongly when the plaster comes off.
items.why: Unused muscle loses structural proteins and shrinks.

items.q: Explain how the quadriceps extend the knee though none of them attaches to the tibia directly.
model: All four join the quadriceps tendon.
The tendon inserts into the patella.
Below the patella it continues as the patellar ligament.
The ligament attaches to the tibial tuberosity, so pulling it straightens the knee.

items.q: Compare the rectus femoris and the vastus lateralis.
model: Both extend the knee through the quadriceps tendon.
The rectus femoris arises from the hip bone, so it also flexes the thigh.
The vastus lateralis arises from the femur and acts on the knee only.
The rectus femoris lies in front; the vastus lateralis on the outer side.

items.q: Predict what a knee-jerk test shows if the reflex arc is intact.
model: Muscle spindles signal into the spinal cord.
Their fibres excite the motor neuron directly.
The quadriceps contract and the leg kicks forwards.

check.stem: Which quadriceps muscle also flexes the thigh at the hip?
check.why: The rectus femoris arises from the hip bone, so it also helps raise the knee (flex the thigh).

check.stem: Where does the patellar ligament attach?
check.why: The patellar ligament attaches to the tibial tuberosity.

check.stem: Which group opposes the quadriceps at the knee?
check.why: The hamstrings flex the leg, whereas the quadriceps extend it.
